content: Decorin is a protein encoded by the DCN gene in humans. It is classified as a proteoglycan with an average molecular weight ranging from 90 to 140 kilodaltons (kDa). This protein belongs to the small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP) family and is composed of a protein core containing leucine-rich repeats, along with a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chain. The GAG chain can be either chondroitin sulfate (CS) or dermatan sulfate (DS). Decorin is a small proteoglycan found in the cellular or pericellular matrix and shares structural similarities with the protein biglycan. It is believed that decorin and biglycan arose from a gene duplication event. Decorin is a key component of connective tissue, where it binds to type I collagen fibrils and plays a critical role in the assembly of the extracellular matrix. The name decorin is derived from its ability to decorate type I collagen and its interaction with the d and e bands of collagen fibrils. Functionally, decorin influences fibrillogenesis and interacts with various molecules, including fibronectin, thrombospondin, complement component C1q, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta). It has been shown to either enhance or inhibit the activity of TGF-beta1. Decorin's primary function involves regulation during the cell cycle. It is also implicated in the regulation of autophagy, endothelial cell function, and the inhibition of angiogenesis. This anti-angiogenic effect is mediated through a high-affinity interaction with vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2), which leads to increased expression of the tumor suppressor gene PEG3. Additionally, decorin inhibits other angiogenic growth factors, such as angiopoietin, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF). Recent studies have identified decorin as a myokine, a type of protein secreted by muscle cells. In this role, it promotes muscle hypertrophy by binding to and inhibiting myostatin. Clinically, decorin expression is reduced in keloid scars compared to healthy skin. In animal studies, the infusion of decorin into experimental rodent spinal cord injuries has been shown to suppress scar formation and promote axon growth. Decorin also exhibits anti-tumorigenic properties in experimental murine tumor models and can suppress the growth of various tumor cell lines. The decorin gene is known to produce multiple alternatively spliced transcript variants. Mutations in the decorin gene are associated with congenital stromal corneal dystrophy, a rare genetic disorder affecting the cornea. Decorin has been shown to interact with several molecules, including type I collagen, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), TGF-beta1, Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4).
